slides.title: Context shapes a plain reading (1 of 2)
body: Taking Jesus seriously does not mean looking for hinges when He calls Himself the door. In John 10 He uses a shepherd-and-sheep image to explain entry and salvation through Him. The surrounding speech tells us how to understand the image.

readings.text: So Jesus again said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep. All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them. I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture.
readings.relation: In this shepherd-and-sheep discourse, Jesus explains entry and salvation through Him. The metaphor is understood from that context.

slides.notes: Taking Jesus seriously does not mean looking for hinges when He calls Himself the door. In John 10 He uses a shepherd-and-sheep image to explain entry and salvation through Him. The surrounding speech tells us how to understand the image.
slides.originalScript:

Source: Sentinel_aee5278884948191a6296646bb047e4f (2026-10-20)

Before we begin, I want to make my purpose absolutely clear. My purpose is to help you know God.

We are aliens in a foreign land. And whether we realize it or not, we bring assumptions about God from the way we grew up and the culture around us. Every misconception His Word corrects is a blessing. Every correction helps us know Him better.

Honestly, it shocks me how many intelligent, mature Christians are comfortable with God using millions of years of evolution to create living things. But I’m not saying that disagreeing with me about creation means you don’t belong to Christ. I am asking us to examine what we believe, and why.

The authority I’m speaking with today is not my own. I don’t want you to believe something just because I say it. I want us to let Scripture interpret Scripture.

That means reading what’s there, in context. When Jesus says, “I am the door,” taking Him seriously doesn’t mean imagining hinges. It means understanding what He is saying. We need that same care when we open Genesis.

So here’s the central question: Do you take God at His Word?

Not, “Do you agree with Phil?” Are we willing to let God’s Word correct us, even when it challenges something we’ve believed for years?
slides.editorialNotes: This is the recovered complete prior introduction. A plain reading considers genre and context. Do not claim every biblical use of good means moral perfection.
slides.claimNote: Applying contextual reading to Genesis is a method. John 10 does not decide the genre or chronology of Genesis.

body: That is how I want to approach Genesis too: read the passage in its setting, notice its genre, and compare related passages. The presence of figurative language in one passage does not, by itself, decide the genre or chronology of another. My interpretation remains accountable to the text.

slides.title: Evolution is real.
body: Evolution is a proven, observable, undeniable fact of God's creation. Now, before anybody panics, what do I mean? Heritable characteristics of populations change across generations. We observe variation, inheritance and natural selection. I believe the God who made creatures made them capable of adaptation.

I’m also part of the catholic church. Did you guys know that? What do we mean in the Apostles’ Creed by the holy catholic church? Universal. Where does your head go? Often to the Roman Catholic Church. Terminology matters. We need to know what claim we are actually talking about.

slides.title: Different words, different questions (1 of 2)
body: When I spoke with Ben about evolution, he thought first about stars and planets. Someone else hears the same word and pictures human ancestry. Those are different subjects. Cosmic development concerns the history of the universe. Biological evolution concerns changes in living populations and the ancestry of organisms. Abiogenesis concerns the origin of the first life.

slides.claimNote: Definitions explain the positions under discussion. A Christian may accept biological common ancestry while affirming a Creator.
slides.originalScript: When I spoke with Ben about evolution, he thought first about stars and planets. Someone else hears the same word and pictures human ancestry. Those are different subjects. Cosmic development concerns the history of the universe. Biological evolution concerns changes in living populations and the ancestry of organisms. Abiogenesis concerns the origin of the first life. Philosophical naturalism makes a further claim about reality and the absence of a Creator. These subjects can connect in someone’s worldview, but they are not interchangeable. A Christian who accepts common ancestry has not therefore said that God does not exist. I disagree with that Christian’s reading of creation, but I must represent the position accurately.

slides.title: More time — or an organizing mechanism? (1 of 2)
body: Frank has a helpful illustration here. Picture red, white and blue confetti falling from a plane. Would giving it a longer fall explain an American flag laid out on your lawn? The point I appreciate is that more time alone is not an organizing mechanism. That is an illustration about explanation and design, not a probability calculation.

One really great part of it, and by the way, Frank Turek and I agree on a lot of things here, but I disagree with him that death for animals can exist before the fall of man. Well, what it really is, is that the death of animals can't exist before day six. That's really what my argument is. So yeah, it doesn't matter how old the Earth is, right? What really matters is, when does death enter into the world, and what does God call very good? So yeah, but Frank Turek has this amazing analogy in this YouTube video about dropping confetti, red, white, and blue confetti from a plane at 5,000 feet of elevation and then 10,000 feet. Adding more time for the confetti to fall isn't going to increase the chances of it forming the American flag on your front lawn. It's going to increase the chance of failure, if anything.

slides.title: Six days. A completed, very good creation. (1 of 2)
body: I read Genesis as six ordinary days. The numbered days, repeated evenings and mornings, and Exodus’s creation-workweek connection matter to my reading. But I want my central point clear: I am not trying to prove a numerical age for Earth today. I am asking what belongs in the completed creation God calls very good.

readings.text: For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy.
readings.relation: The Sabbath command explicitly relates six days of creation and the seventh day of rest to Israel’s work pattern.

slides.title: One ordered creation week (1 of 2)
body: Notice the correspondences between the first three days and the next three. Light and darkness correspond with the lights governing day and night. Waters and sky correspond with sea creatures and birds. Land and vegetation correspond with land animals and humanity. These pairings help us pay attention to the account’s order.

slides.title: Vegetation on day three; food on day six (1 of 2)
body: Genesis 1:9–13 places land and vegetation bearing seed and fruit on day three. The food assignment quoted here comes later, at the end of day six. Verse 29 addresses the people God has made.

I love the provision in that picture: plants, seed and fruit given for food. A fruit tree can feed someone and continue growing, bearing again in another season. I want to notice that provision without mixing up the days or the subjects of the verses.

readings.text: And God said, “Behold, I have given you every plant yielding seed that is on the face of all the earth, and every tree with seed in its fruit. You shall have them for food.
readings.relation: Verse 29 assigns plant food to humanity on day six. The earlier appearance of vegetation is described in Genesis 1:9–13.

slides.claimNote: The quote concerns human food. Reading it alongside day-three vegetation is a contextual comparison, not a claim that the food speech occurs on day three.
slides.originalScript: Here the land appears and vegetation bears seed and fruit. I love the provision in that picture. A fruit tree can feed a creature and continue growing, bearing again in another season. Animals can also disperse some seeds after eating fruit. There is beauty in that relationship. I am not saying every seed survives every animal, or that no plant cells die. Plants are living organisms. I am saying we should notice the distinction between plants given for food and the question of animal suffering and death. God’s power is not the limitation. The question is what kind of provision He describes in the world He calls good.

slides.title: Very good (1 of 2)
body: Here is the assessment I keep returning to: very good. God looks at everything He has made and approves His completed creation. What belongs inside that declaration? I believe it is difficult to place animal starvation, disease, predation, and death before human rebellion and then call that the means by which God established His original good world.

readings.text: And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good. And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day.
readings.relation: God evaluates everything He has made and calls the completed creation very good. The verse also identifies the sixth day.

But I do not want to pretend these two words settle every question by themselves. A tree being good does not mean the tree has kept the commandments. Goodness in a created thing and moral righteousness in a person are related but distinct questions. Let the food provisions and the wider biblical story help us examine the claim.

slides.title: Finished work. A day of rest. (1 of 2)
body: Do not let the chapter number stop you. Genesis 2:1–3 completes the creation account. God finishes His work, ceases from it and blesses the seventh day. The rest marks completion. Exodus draws on this pattern for Israel’s work and Sabbath.

I appreciate that God gives His people a rhythm. We are creatures who work and need rest. His completed creation gives us something to receive with gratitude rather than treating life as an endless attempt to prove everything depends on us.

readings.text: And on the seventh day God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done. So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it God rested from all his work that he had done in creation.
readings.relation: This account states completion, rest and blessing. Its wording gives the creation-work pattern rather than a medical description of tiredness.

slides.title: From the whole world to the garden
body: Read the accounts together. Genesis 1 presents the broad account of creation. Genesis 2:4 introduces the following garden account, drawing close to the man, God’s command and marriage. I describe that change of focus as a close-up.

It is an explanation of the account’s movement, not a phrase the verse itself supplies. The change of focus does not settle every question about sequence, genre or translation. The passage deserves more careful reading than either a quick dismissal or a slogan.

readings.text: These are the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created, in the day that the LORD God made the earth and the heavens.
readings.relation: This verse introduces the generations of the heavens and earth and the following garden account.

slides.claimNote: Describing Genesis 2 as a close-up is an interpretive explanation of its focus, not a quotation from the verse.
slides.originalScript: Read the accounts together. The change in focus does not itself resolve every question about sequence, genre or translation. The account brings the hearer close to humanity’s place, God’s command, the garden and marriage. Do not bring back the withdrawn claim that Genesis 1 is indisputably classic Hebrew poetry, or the false etymology that universe means one spoken word. Neither claim is needed here.

slides.title: The command before disobedience (1 of 4)
body: Genesis gives the man a command before the account of rebellion. He may eat from the garden’s trees, with a prohibition concerning the tree of the knowledge of good and evil and a warning about death.

Read this warning in its own place in the story. It establishes human accountability to the Creator. The issue is not that people lacked enough information to win a debate. They were responsible to hear and obey God.

readings.text: And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, “You may surely eat of every tree of the garden, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die.”
readings.relation: This is the command and warning before the transgression. It does not itself narrate the later ground curse or painful toil.

slides.notes: Genesis gives the man a command before the account of rebellion. He may eat from the garden’s trees, with a prohibition concerning the tree of the knowledge of good and evil and a warning about death. Read this warning in its own place in the story. It establishes human accountability to the Creator. The issue is not that people lacked enough information to win a debate. They were responsible to hear and obey God.
slides.claimNote: The command concerns the man’s obedience and the threatened consequence. It is distinct from the judgment pronounced after the transgression.
slides.originalScript: Genesis 3 describes rebellion against the Creator. The issue is not that people lacked enough information to win a debate. They disobeyed God. Judgment follows, the ground is cursed, toil becomes painful, and the man is told he will return to dust. The account changes the way we understand the world we inhabit. Our present experience is not simply the original creation continuing untouched. There is beauty, but there is also rupture. There is provision, but also pain. As we read onward, we should pay attention to the connection between human rebellion and the world’s brokenness without claiming that Genesis answers every question about the chronology of all evil.

slides.title: Human rebellion in the narrative (2 of 4)
body: Genesis 3 then describes taking and eating the prohibited fruit. The narrative presents disobedience, not merely an intellectual misunderstanding. I want us to hear that moral claim. It reaches beyond whether we are skilled at explaining creation.

We stand before the Creator as people accountable to Him. The following judgments belong to the account’s response to that transgression, so we should read the action and its consequences in sequence.

readings.text: So when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate.
readings.relation: This verse records the taking, eating and giving of the fruit. The command appears earlier, and the spoken judgments follow.

slides.title: Cursed ground and painful toil (3 of 4)
body: The judgment concerning the man names his disobedience and the ground’s curse. Painful toil changes the way we understand the world we inhabit. Our present experience is not simply the original creation continuing untouched.

There is beauty and provision, but also pain and rupture. This is one of the narrative connections I bring into the larger theological argument. I must still distinguish what this judgment actually states from a complete chronology of every creature’s suffering.

slides.title: The return to dust (4 of 4)
body: The man is told that he will return to the ground from which he was taken. That human return to dust matters to the Bible’s later discussion of Adam and Christ.

I want us to pay attention to the connection between human rebellion and our mortality without claiming that Genesis supplies every biological date we might ask for. The narrative’s judgment is serious, and it prepares us to hear why humanity needs redemption.

slides.title: Adam and Christ (1 of 2)
body: Romans 5 connects sin entering through one man with death spreading to humanity. Paul is explaining our relationship to Adam and our need for Christ. This passage matters enormously to the gospel. Adam’s disobedience and Christ’s obedience are not disconnected ideas. But notice the precision: Romans 5 directly discusses human sin and human death.

readings.text: Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned—
readings.relation: Paul connects Adam’s disobedience and death spreading to humanity with Christ’s obedience and the making righteous of many.

The strong point we must not lose is the one Paul does make: humanity needs the righteousness and life that come through Christ. We cannot repair Adam’s problem by congratulating ourselves on our own goodness.

slides.title: Creation groans and waits (1 of 2)
body: Romans 8 widens our attention to creation itself. Paul describes futility, groaning, and the hope of liberation from corruption. He connects that hope with the revealing of God’s children and the redemption of our bodies. That gives us a way to look honestly at suffering without treating it as the last truth about the world.

readings.text: For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God.
readings.relation: Paul describes creation’s subjection to futility and promised freedom from corruption.

slides.notes: Romans 8 widens our attention to creation itself. Paul describes futility, groaning, and the hope of liberation from corruption. He connects that hope with the revealing of God’s children and the redemption of our bodies. That gives us a way to look honestly at suffering without treating it as the last truth about the world.

He connects that hope with the revealing of God’s children and the redemption of our bodies. That gives us a way to look honestly at suffering without treating it as the last truth about the world. The groaning is real. The hope is real too. This is one of the passages I bring into my larger argument about the Fall and creation’s brokenness. I do not want to isolate one verse and force it to answer everything. I want us to hear the movement from bondage toward the freedom God promises.

slides.title: My central question about animal death (1 of 2)
body: What really matters in my argument is when death enters the world and what God calls very good. I do not place animal death before the completed sixth day. That is my reading of the original food provision, God’s assessment and the Bible’s movement through Fall and redemption. I also connect animal suffering with the fallen world in my broader theological argument.

That is my reading of the original food provision, God’s assessment and the Bible’s movement through Fall and redemption. I also connect animal suffering with the fallen world in my broader theological argument.
slides.originalScript: One really great part of it, and by the way, Frank Turek and I agree on a lot of things here, but I disagree with him that death for animals can exist before the fall of man. Well, what it really is, is that the death of animals can't exist before day six. That's really what my argument is. So yeah, it doesn't matter how old the Earth is, right? What really matters is, when does death enter into the world, and what does God call very good? So yeah, but Frank Turek has this amazing analogy in this YouTube video about dropping confetti, red, white, and blue confetti from a plane at 5,000 feet of elevation and then 10,000 feet. Adding more time for the confetti to fall isn't going to increase the chances of it forming the American flag on your front lawn. It's going to increase the chance of failure, if anything.
slides.editorialNotes: The latest wording focuses on no animal death before completion of day six. Do not silently replace it with a numerical-age proof or claim that Romans 5 explicitly discusses all animals.
slides.claimNote: Theological inference: my no-animal-death-before-completed-day-six conclusion draws together food provision, “very good,” Fall and redemption. No single cited verse explicitly states the whole conclusion.

slides.title: What does this say about God? (1 of 2)
body: We have reached the heart of why this matters to me. What does our account of creation say about the God who made it? Scripture reveals His holiness, goodness, mercy, justice, wisdom, and love. I do not want to invent a version of goodness that simply mirrors my preferences. I want to ask how the Creator reveals Himself.

slides.title: Admiration and final authority
body: I admire C. S. Lewis. That does not make every conclusion he reached my final authority. In The Problem of Pain he considers animal suffering before humanity, including speculative prehuman evil. He took the problem seriously; I still disagree with his approach.

Augustine also reminds us that different readings of creation days predate Darwin. Admiration does not settle interpretation. Not Lewis. Not Augustine. Not your pastor. And certainly not me. Bring the argument back to Scripture. Chronological snobbery cuts both ways: older does not automatically mean false, and newer does not automatically mean wiser.

slides.title: Three questions about death (1 of 2)
body: Am I saying every death in this fallen world is a moral evil? No. God’s judgment is righteous. Ezekiel calls the wicked to turn and live and says God takes no pleasure in their death.

We can affirm justice without celebrating death itself as our final good. Genesis 9 also permits animals for food. That is a different question from cruelty, and a different question from original creation.

readings.text: Say to them, As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live; turn back, turn back from your evil ways, for why will you die, O house of Israel?
readings.relation: Ezekiel explicitly calls the wicked to turn and live rather than depicting God as delighting in their death. Genesis explicitly permits animals for food.

slides.title: Three questions about death (2 of 2)
body: Here are the distinctions I want us to keep: what belonged to the world God originally called very good, what God justly judges after rebellion, and what He permits for food in the fallen world.

slides.title: The question turns toward us (1 of 4)
body: My main purpose is to help you understand what God means when He says good. Have you heard the story of the rich young ruler? Now I want this to get personal.

It is possible to defend six days passionately and still resist what God says about your own sin. The man in Mark wants eternal life and addresses Jesus as good teacher. Jesus turns his attention toward God’s unique goodness. The question reaches beyond winning an argument about the beginning.

readings.text: And as he was setting out on his journey, a man ran up and knelt before him and asked him, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” And Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.
readings.relation: This is the man’s question and Jesus’ reply in the encounter. It opens a discussion of God’s goodness and the man’s allegiance.

slides.title: A claim to goodness meets a costly call (2 of 4)
body: Jesus names commandments concerning our life with other people. The man says he has kept them from his youth. Read that claim in the unfolding encounter, rather than treating his statement as Jesus’ declaration that the man has achieved sinless righteousness.
The next part of the story will expose what he is unwilling to surrender. This helps explain why I want our creation discussion to lead toward our own relationship with the Creator.

slides.title: Will he follow Jesus? (3 of 4)
body: Jesus looks at him and loves him, then calls him to a costly act of trust and to follow. The man leaves sorrowful because he has great possessions. The issue reaches his allegiance. What does he prize more than following Christ?
I want that question to reach me too. God’s goodness is not a way to congratulate myself. It exposes the depth of my need and asks what I am unwilling to place under His authority.

slides.title: Christ died and rose (1 of 2)
body: Paul’s Gospel includes Christ’s death for sins, burial and resurrection. He is reminding the Corinthians of the message he received and delivered to them. The resurrection is essential to that message. It is not a decorative ending to a creation talk.

slides.title: The curse will not remain (1 of 2)
body: Our hope reaches beyond forgiveness alone. Christ will raise His people. God will dwell with them. Death, mourning, and the curse will not rule forever. The promised future is not merely that we stop asking questions about the past. It is life with our Creator in a world no longer broken by sin.

readings.text: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away.”
readings.relation: The promised new creation removes death and mourning, and the curse will be gone.

slides.notes: Our hope reaches beyond forgiveness alone. Christ will raise His people. God will dwell with them. Death, mourning, and the curse will not rule forever. The promised future is not merely that we stop asking questions about the past. It is life with our Creator in a world no longer broken by sin.
slides.claimNote: Future restoration is explicit. It is not a detailed specification of every aspect of Eden’s biology or the intermediate state.
slides.originalScript: Our hope reaches beyond forgiveness alone. Christ will raise His people. God will dwell with them. Death, mourning, and the curse will not rule forever. The promised future is not merely that we stop asking questions about the past. It is life with our Creator in a world no longer broken by sin. That hope changes how we face suffering now. We can grieve without pretending death is harmless, and we can trust without pretending we understand every detail. The One through whom all things were made is faithful to complete His saving work. This is the hope I want us to carry from the beginning of Scripture toward its promised end.

body: I would like to hear your questions. We do not need to pretend we have resolved every issue. Which passage would you like to examine more closely? Where did an interpretive step need more explanation? What do you understand very good to mean in its context? How do you connect Genesis 3, Romans 8, and the promised removal of the curse?

We can also ask a more personal question: where do we rely on our own goodness instead of God’s grace? Please feel free to disagree and show us the text behind your answer. I want a conversation that helps us know God and understand His Word more faithfully.

slides.title: Day 1: light and darkness (1 of 2)
body: One thing that stops me here is the separation of light and darkness before the day-four account of the lights. I do not fully understand that. I want to be able to say so without treating my uncertainty as a defect in Scripture. The passage tells us what God does; it does not answer every physical question we can ask.

readings.text: And God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. And God saw that the light was good. And God separated the light from the darkness. God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And there was evening and there was morning, the first day.
readings.relation: The account names light, separation of light and darkness, evening and morning, and the first day.

slides.title: Day 2: waters and expanse (1 of 2)
body: When I first read this, I pictured a water canopy or perhaps clouds. Then I kept reading about the lights in the expanse and the birds flying across it, and I began reconsidering what I was picturing. Is sky the best English description here? Are we thinking too narrowly if we insist on one modern physical category?

readings.text: And God said, “Let there be an expanse in the midst of the waters, and let it separate the waters from the waters.” And God made the expanse and separated the waters that were under the expanse from the waters that were above the expanse. And it was so.
readings.relation: This is the text’s distinction between the waters and the expanse. Later lights and birds are described in Genesis 1:14–20.

slides.notes: When I first read this, I pictured a water canopy or perhaps clouds. Then I kept reading about the lights in the expanse and the birds flying across it, and I began reconsidering what I was picturing. Is sky the best English description here? Are we thinking too narrowly if we insist on one modern physical category?
slides.claimNote: Canopy, cloud, sky and outer-space models go beyond what these verses specify. Psalm 148:4 is another waters-above reference, not a technical mechanism.
slides.originalScript: When I first read this, I pictured a water canopy or perhaps clouds. Then I kept reading about the lights in the expanse and the birds flying across it, and I began reconsidering what I was picturing. Is sky the best English description here? Are we thinking too narrowly if we insist on one modern physical category? I want Scripture to interpret Scripture. We can compare the Flood account and Psalm 148. But the comparison does not authorize us to claim that Genesis explicitly describes a vapor canopy that later collapsed. That would be a hypothesis. The useful starting point is the distinction the passage actually makes between the waters and the expanse.

slides.title: Day 4: lights and appointed times (1 of 2)
body: If you have the opportunity to stand under a truly dark sky, do it. Pictures do not replace that experience for me. Look through a telescope if you can. The heavens draw my attention to the glory of their Maker. Genesis describes lights marking times and illuminating the earth.

readings.text: And God said, “Let there be lights in the expanse of the heavens to separate the day from the night. And let them be for signs and for seasons, and for days and years, and let them be lights in the expanse of the heavens to give light upon the earth.” And it was so.
readings.relation: The account describes the lights’ functions and the greater and lesser lights.

slides.originalScript: If you have the opportunity to stand under a truly dark sky, do it. Pictures do not replace that experience for me. Look through a telescope if you can. The heavens draw my attention to the glory of their Maker. Genesis describes lights marking times and illuminating the earth. slides.title: Day 5: life fills the waters and sky (1 of 2)
body: The waters teem with living creatures and birds fly above the earth. Notice the blessing. God addresses His creatures with fruitfulness and multiplication. He cares about the life He has made. This develops the connection with the waters and sky described earlier. I also notice the repeated references to kinds and goodness.

readings.text: So God created the great sea creatures and every living creature that moves, with which the waters swarm, according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. And God saw that it was good. And God blessed them, saying, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters in the seas, and let birds multiply on the earth.”
readings.relation: These verses state the creation of sea creatures and birds and God’s blessing of fruitfulness.

slides.title: Day 6: animals and humanity (1 of 2)
body: Genesis describes land animals and humanity made in God’s image. Our worth and accountability are grounded in our relationship to our Maker. I read these as belonging to the same creation day.

slides.title: Dinosaurs: what are we claiming? (1 of 2)
body: Dinosaurs are exciting. Their size and variety make us stop and look. I want that wonder in this presentation, but I also want us to know exactly what we are claiming. Genesis does not use the modern word dinosaur. Identifying Job’s Behemoth or Leviathan with a particular extinct species is debated.

readings.text: “Behold, Behemoth, which I made as I made you; he eats grass like an ox.
readings.relation: Job names Behemoth and describes it; it does not provide a modern scientific species name.

slides.claimNote: Identifying Behemoth or Leviathan with a particular dinosaur remains uncertain. An imagined picture cannot establish coexistence.
slides.originalScript: Dinosaurs are exciting. Their size and variety make us stop and look. I want that wonder in this presentation, but I also want us to know exactly what we are claiming. Genesis does not use the modern word dinosaur. Identifying Job’s Behemoth or Leviathan with a particular extinct species is debated. An artist can show a human beside a giant animal, but the artwork is not the evidence. If we are going to discuss fossils, chronology, or Job’s creatures in detail, we need to examine those arguments on their own terms. For this devotional, keep the central connection clear: I believe God made the land animals and humanity, and I want to understand that claim faithfully.

slides.title: The lifespans recorded in Genesis (1 of 2)
body: We should also examine the way we dismiss ancient people. Genesis records Adam’s lifespan as nine hundred thirty years, Noah’s as nine hundred fifty, and Shem’s as six hundred in total. I take these as accounts of real people. Imagine the experience a person could accumulate across centuries. That is a possibility worth considering.

readings.text: Thus all the days that Adam lived were 930 years, and he died.
readings.relation: The ages are recorded in these genealogical passages.

readings.text: All the days of Noah were 950 years, and he died.

slides.claimNote: Ages are textual data; extraordinary IQ, disease mechanisms and universal ancient superiority are not supplied by these verses.
slides.originalScript: We should also examine the way we dismiss ancient people. Genesis records Adam’s lifespan as nine hundred thirty years, Noah’s as nine hundred fifty, and Shem’s as six hundred in total. I take these as accounts of real people. Imagine the experience a person could accumulate across centuries. That is a possibility worth considering. Scripture does not give us their IQ scores or a medical mechanism for their longevity. So I am not using these bars to prove that everyone then was more intelligent than everyone now. I am using them to challenge our habit of assuming ancient means foolish. And across those long lives, there is still a sobering reality: death comes.

slides.title: Older does not mean foolish (1 of 2)
body: We have remarkable tools and accumulated knowledge. That does not make us automatically wiser about God. We should not assume an older belief is false simply because it is old, or that a new idea is true simply because it sounds modern. The reverse error is possible too. A claim does not become true because it has a long tradition behind it.
slides.notes: We have remarkable tools and accumulated knowledge. That does not make us automatically wiser about God. We should not assume an older belief is false simply because it is old, or that a new idea is true simply because it sounds modern. The reverse error is possible too. A claim does not become true because it has a long tradition behind it.
slides.claimNote: Chronological snobbery is a reasoning caution. A belief’s age alone establishes neither its truth nor its falsehood.
slides.originalScript: We have remarkable tools and accumulated knowledge. That does not make us automatically wiser about God. We should not assume an older belief is false simply because it is old, or that a new idea is true simply because it sounds modern. The reverse error is possible too. A claim does not become true because it has a long tradition behind it. I want us to examine the reasons. When we read Genesis, let us avoid treating its people as fools merely because they lived long ago. Our phones may be newer. That does not mean our instincts about the Creator are beyond correction. Humility belongs to serious inquiry, including Christian inquiry.

slides.title: Common ancestry is a branching claim
body: That familiar picture of an ape gradually standing upright can give the wrong impression. The scientific claim is not that humans descended from the chimpanzees alive today. It is that humans and other living apes share ancestors. That is why a branching diagram is more accurate than a parade ending with a modern person.

The broader common-ancestry claim extends across living things beyond the human-and-ape comparison. I reject universal common ancestry, but I do not help my argument by attacking a position scientists are not actually asserting. Understanding the claim fairly gives us a better starting point for asking where the evidence and the interpretation lead.

slides.title: The last enemy (1 of 2)
body: First Corinthians 15 calls death an enemy. Paul places its defeat within the victory of the risen Christ and the resurrection of His people. This is not a small detail attached to an origins discussion. It is Christian hope. Death does not get the final word over those who belong to Jesus.

readings.text: The last enemy to be destroyed is death.
readings.relation: Paul explicitly identifies death as the last enemy to be destroyed in Christ’s resurrection victory.

This is not a small detail attached to an origins discussion. It is Christian hope. Death does not get the final word over those who belong to Jesus.

This is not a small detail attached to an origins discussion. It is Christian hope. Death does not get the final word over those who belong to Jesus. That is one reason the place of death in the original creation concerns me. I see a movement in Scripture in which Christ overcomes what destroys and corrupts. I want to understand the beginning in the light of that promised victory. And I want our discussion to lead toward worship of the risen Savior rather than ending with a clever argument about the past.

slides.title: The Bible’s connected story
body: Creation. Rebellion. Curse. Redemption. Resurrection. Restoration. These are connected movements in the biblical story. God creates. People rebel. Judgment and curse follow. God acts to redeem through Christ. Christ rises, and His people will rise. The promised end includes the removal of death and the curse. I believe this pattern helps us examine the place of suffering and death in the beginning.

It also keeps us from treating Genesis as disposable background. The beginning matters because the same Creator is working toward the promised end. But keep the gospel at the center: the story reaches us as people who need rescue, not merely as observers who need an interesting explanation.

slides.title: Good through suffering (1 of 2)
body: I need to make an important distinction here. I am not saying God can never permit suffering for a good purpose. Look at the cross. The people who crucified Jesus acted wickedly, and yet their wickedness did not defeat God’s saving purpose. God brings good through suffering. Christians also know that trials can produce endurance.

It does not tell us exactly which modern taxonomic rank Genesis means by kinds. A car and a bicycle sharing wheels can illustrate my common-designer intuition, but the analogy by itself does not disprove common ancestry.

slides.title: Selection stories need clear labels
body: Imagine a zebra with an unusual stripe colour. Whether that variation helps it survive and reproduce depends on its environment and other factors. This is a hypothetical teaching example, not a report of a zebra population we observed.
I do not mean that all mutations are harmful or that every gene belongs in a simple strong-versus-weak hierarchy. The example helps us ask what selection does; it does not settle the origin of life.

slides.title: If one year were one second…
body: Suppose every year were represented by one second. How long would a thousand years take? About 16.7 minutes. A million would take about 11.6 days, and a billion about 31.7 years. The change of scale makes these intervals easier to picture.
It does not tell us which chronology is true, and a number does not become impossible simply because it surprises us. We still need evidence and a clear account of the process under discussion.

body: The 1980 Mount St Helens eruption and the landscape changes that followed provide documented examples of rapid local processes. That matters when we ask how quickly a particular feature could form. But material, scale and physical mechanism matter too.

This local example cannot by itself date every rock, demonstrate a worldwide Flood correlation or invalidate isotope dating. I want the illustration to show what the observation supports, without asking it to prove much more.

slides.title: Different clocks answer different questions
body: Radiocarbon is one radiometric method, used for relatively recent once-living material. Other isotope systems address much older material. A criticism needs to identify the sample, method and relevant assumptions.

Contamination, reservoir effects and initial conditions are real questions to investigate. They are not a reason to pretend that carbon 14 measures dinosaur-age rocks as billions of years old, or that one anomalous result refutes every dating method.

Do not repeat claims that radiocarbon dates are billions of years off or that there is no evidence of life older than 10000 years.

I am not claiming that every seed survives, that manure is built into a seed, or that plant cells never die. Plants are living organisms. My illustration helps us notice the food provision while we examine the separate question about animal suffering.

Dragon artwork and dictionary stories also do not by themselves prove coexistence. The proposed glass-lizard identity for the Eden serpent remains a side theory, not a biblical identification. My gospel argument does not depend on resolving those creature questions.

slides.title: Eight people and a Chinese character?

That linguistic claim would need specialist evidence. The idea that ancestor worship began with long-lived patriarchs is likewise speculation, and a proposed Flood–Younger Dryas equivalence has not been established here. I am preserving these research questions without teaching them as discoveries.

body: My brother Tim is a lawyer. Thinking about the difference between making a law and interpreting one helps me ask philosophical questions about the world’s regularities. Yet a natural law is not the same thing as a civil statute.

Mars-rover precision shows the effectiveness of scientific investigation; it does not prove that all science began with Christians. I can express my wonder at the heavens without attributing an unverified quotation to a famous Christian thinker.

He was not claiming that God required millions of years. Chronological snobbery warns against dismissing a belief merely for its age, but age alone cannot establish truth either. Admiration does not relieve us of examining an argument.

slides.title: A conditional either-or challenge
body: I want to preserve the seriousness of taking God’s Word as true. If Genesis intends six ordinary days, that reading cannot at the same time mean a contrary chronology. But the interpretive premise has to be argued.

The choice is not simply agree with Phil or reject God. Christians can dispute genre and the days while affirming biblical authority and Christ. My challenge is to examine the text honestly, not to turn agreement with me into a salvation requirement.

slides.title: Scripture can describe a good man (2 of 2)
body: Acts calls Barnabas a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith. That should stop me from treating every biblical use of good as a claim of absolute sinlessness. Mark 10 directs the rich man toward God’s unique goodness, while Acts describes Barnabas’s character and life.
Neither passage gives me a reason to boast that I have earned salvation. God’s sinless righteousness, genuine human good and created goodness need to be understood in their own contexts.

slides.title: A conversation, not a loyalty test
body: I want this to be a conversation that helps us know God. Show the text behind a claim. Allow an honest question. If my interpretation needs correcting, show me why. The purpose is not to sort the room into people loyal to Phil and people who are not.

The Gospel remains central: the Creator is the One against whom we have sinned, and Christ is the One we need. Creation chronology is a serious discussion, but agreement with my chronology is not the condition of belonging to Him.

slides.title: Two views. One nearby star. (1 of 2)
body: Start with an intentionally unscaled thumb demonstration: hold up a thumb against a farther background, alternate eyes and notice the apparent change in direction. The thumb does not move; the viewing position changes. Now replace the eyes with Earth’s positions on opposite sides of its orbit, about six months apart. One star’s apparent position is compared with the more distant stellar background.

The thumb does not move; the viewing position changes. Now replace the eyes with Earth’s positions on opposite sides of its orbit, about six months apart. One star’s apparent position is compared with the more distant stellar background. The conventional parallax angle p corresponds to the one-AU radius, not the whole two-AU baseline. The maximum opposite-view shift is about 2 p. Actual measurements account for proper motion and other effects; a classroom triangle is an introduction, not the entire data-reduction process. Never use the Sun as something to look at for this demonstration.

slides.title: Ten feet here. Proxima far away.
body: Use the primary room-sized demonstration first. Put the students’ eye positions ten feet apart and a Sun marker halfway between, five feet from each. Those two eye positions represent Earth’s opposite orbital positions, a full baseline of 2 AU. If the target represents Proxima Centauri at approximately 4.25 light-years, its scaled distance would be about 254 miles, or 409 km.

A wall or stage prop across the room is therefore not a scale-correct Proxima target. Use the diagram to explain the long narrow triangle. This is a proportional geometry model, not an actual line of sight over Earth’s curved surface. The background reference is farther stars, not the Sun.

Ok, go into my free market wildlife Philip Aram sermon’s tab and create a new sermon named “Devotional: Creation”

And I want you to help me organize my thoughts here: CREATION DEVOTIONAL


If you read Darwin’s Origin of Species, all of God’s order & design in organisms are attributed to death & suffering.




The main question to ask yourself:   God said on Day 6 (gen 1:31),  God saw all that he had made, and it was very good. And there was evening, and there was morning—the sixth day.

So, could there have been any death or suffering before day 6?

Is death good in God’s point of view?
Is suffering good in God’s point of view?


If everything was good on day 6, could death & suffering have existed?

We discover the correct interpretation when scripture interprets scripture for us. Jesus, Peter, and Paul, interpret the creation story for us. We can take their word for it. 



It’s perfectly understandable to recognize that God has the power required to make everything through evolution, it’s not a problem of his power, it’s a problem of his character. The question isn’t “Can God do this”, it’s  “would God do this”. If you believe in the God of the 66 book Bible and believe that we have the infallible Word of God available to us in that library we call the Old and New Testament, then you believe a few characteristics of God has been revealed to us:
[list of the attributes of God]

So, is it merciful to have a dinosaur starve to death before the fall? He calls it good on day 6. 
Is it loving to… ect




Creation Devotional:

The Kingdom Dichotomy


I’ve named this devotional “The Kingdom Dichotomy,” and the reason I named it that is because when I was writing this devotional, Pastor George preached out of John 15, where Jesus makes some pretty serious truth claims about what is promised to those who would follow him. He says, 
“If you belonged to the world, it would love you as its own. As it is, you do not belong to the world, but I have chosen you out of the world. That is why the world hates you."


Why is that?


We usually think of Dichotomy as a decision, you’re faced with one decision or the other, and usually, it’s a false binary. There’s an infinite amount of decisions you can make. You can either eat a chick fil a, or in n out, those choices are so good that you don’t even consider McDonald’s or Carl’s Jr. 

Miriam Webster defines dichotomy as, “a division into two mutually exclusive or contradictory groups or entities”


Bits & Pieces:



Belief about human origins	Percentage
God created humans in approximately their present form within the past 10,000 years	37%
Humans evolved over millions of years, with God guiding the process	34%
Humans evolved over millions of years, without God’s involvement	24%
No opinion	5%



Well, here's the thing about the Big Bang model is that everything else about it points to God exploding the universe into one moment. I believe in the Big Bang. I just believe the Big Bang took a day and that God used His power. You know what I mean? Okay, now moving on from that, I do want to clarify this is not the central argument of my devotional. Because this would be getting out in the weeds. This is not my central argument. My central argument is that the Bible declares that God created the heavens and the earth in six days, and at the end of the six days, He said it was good. So can millions of years, can a single death or a single ounce of suffering exist before day six and for it to be good? Do you know what God's level of good is? God's level of good is moral perfection. Here's a fun fact, or not a fun fact. Here's something I want you to take away from here today. Honestly, this is more important than the creationist thing. Okay? This is more important than the six days. Okay? This is of secondary importance. It doesn't mean it's not important. It just means other things do supersede it. Other things do have more importance. And here's something that's more important. I want you to know that God's standard of good means moral perfection. Okay? So if anybody ever asks you out on the street, if anyone ever asks you, Hey, do you think you're a good person? You tell them no. No. Unless you have obtained perfect righteousness, which I just am gonna bet all of my money, everything in the world, that you have not obtained perfect righteousness, that you have not obtained perfect goodness. You are evil. You sin. You're selfish. Even your good deeds are riddled in sin. And when you call yourself a good person, you are being self-righteous. You are being puffed up with pride because you know you're not a good person. You know. You know your failures, and God knows your failures. God is omniscient, and then I'll share a verse about, you know, maybe in Psalm 139, verses, you know, 1 through 8, you know. God is omniscient. He knows your failures. And that's why He sent Jesus Christ, His only begotten Son, to live a perfectly moral, good life. He was perfect. When the rich young ruler came up to Him and asked, you know, blah, blah, blah, good teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life, good teacher? Jesus responds, Why do you call me good? No one is good but God alone. What does that mean? That means if you think you're a good person, you are directly contradicting Jesus Christ. You are not good. You will never be good on this earth, not according to God's standards. But let me give you this hope. Let me give you this hope in salvation. Let me give you this. God has promised in His Word that if you accept Jesus Christ as your Savior, as your atoning sacrifice that took your death and punishment on the cross for you. You know every time you sin, do you know what the Bible says your wages are, what you earn, what you deserve when you sin? Death. The wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus. That's the gospel. If you just repent and turn away from your sins and ask Jesus Christ into your heart, if you ask Jesus Christ to be your Lord and Savior, He is just and willing to forgive. And He doesn't see your wickedness, even though you are wicked. You're evil and you're not perfect. He doesn't see your wickedness. He sees the perfect righteousness of Christ for the rest of your life and for the rest of eternity. And when you enter into heaven, because of the righteousness of Christ, He will make you morally perfect. He will make you perfectly morally good. And He will wipe away every tear. You'll get to enjoy eternity with Him. And that's how I want to end the devotional. That's the point of it. It's not about the science. It's about the gospel. It's about recognizing what God calls good. It's about recognizing what God's standards are. He is high above us. He is in lofty places where we can't reach.




Introduction:

Before we begin, I want to make my goal for this devotional absolutely clear. 

I want every single one of you to walk away today knowing where your allegiance lies.

I want you to confidently answer this question: Do you place your ultimate faith and trust in the Word of God, or in the word of man? 

I want you to know which authority you submit to, which kingdom you belong to.

Because the Bible makes something abundantly clear: there are only two kingdoms. There is the Kingdom of Heaven, whose ruler is God, and the kingdom of this world, whose ruler is Satan.

There is no third kingdom. There is no middle ground. Every single one of you is in the midst of battle, in a war that has waged, I’d argue, roughly 6,000 years.

Jesus Himself said in Matthew 12:30, “Whoever is not with me is against me.” How much clearer could Jesus get? If you do not submit to his word, and his authority, you are submitting to another’s authority; that would be Satan, the ruler of this world.

More than anything, I want you to examine yourself today. Where does your allegiance lie?

We’re going to circle back to that most important question later. But for now, I want to begin with a statement that is absolutely, undeniably the truth.

Evolution is a proven, observable, scientific fact of God’s creation. 







——


Before we move on, I want to tell you something that might surprise you.

One of my favorite Christian thinkers to ever live is C. S. Lewis.

I love C. S. Lewis. I love his writings. I love his defense of the Christian faith.

But did you know that C. S. Lewis accepted the idea that animals were suffering and dying long before Adam ever existed?

In his book The Problem of Pain, Lewis addresses animal suffering, the Fall, and even the possibility that human beings descended physically from earlier animals.

Even the great C.S Lewis fell victim to this snare. I want to make something abundantly clear.

I do not believe the age of the earth is a primary issue of the Christian faith.

What do I mean by that?

There are doctrines that are absolutely foundational to Christianity.

The authority and trustworthiness of Scripture. The deity of Jesus Christ. His virgin birth. His sinless life, His atoning death, and His bodily resurrection.

Salvation by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone.

These are foundational truths.

And I believe that Christians can disagree about the age of the earth and still be brothers and sisters in Christ.

But here’s my concern.

When does our interpretation of Genesis begin to undermine our understanding of the rest of Scripture?

Because I believe the question of death before the Fall gets dangerously close to that line.

And I want you to understand why.

How do we reconcile millions of years of animal suffering, disease, predation, and extinction with God’s declaration that His completed creation was very good?

How do we reconcile that with the curse in Genesis 3?

With the groaning of creation in Romans 8?

With Paul’s declaration in 1 Corinthians 15 that death is the last enemy to be destroyed?

And with God’s promise in Revelation that death will be no more?

These aren’t insignificant questions!

These are questions that reach from the very first chapters of Genesis to the very last chapters of Revelation.

And I believe that attempts to reconcile millions of years of death before Adam with Scripture require some very difficult interpretive decisions.

But don’t just take my word for it.

I don’t want you to believe something simply because I believe it.

I don’t want you to believe something because C. S. Lewis believed it.

Or because John Calvin believed it.

Or Martin Luther.

Or your pastor.

I want you to believe what God has revealed in His Word.

So we’re going to take a journey through Scripture.

We’re going to begin in Genesis.

We’re going to look at the six days of creation.

We’re going to examine the Fall of Adam and Eve.

We’re going to look at Noah and the Flood.

We’re going to visit Job and read about Behemoth and Leviathan.

We’re going to examine what Jesus Himself said about creation, marriage, Adam, and the days of Noah.

We’re going to read what Paul taught about sin and death.

And finally, we’re going to look ahead to the new heavens and the new earth, where God promises that death will be no more.

And throughout this journey, I want you to keep one question in mind.

If God originally created the world through millions of years of death and suffering, why does the Bible describe death as an enemy that Christ came to defeat?

That’s the question I want us to investigate.

We’ve spent some time discussing how mankind understands the history of the world.

But this isn’t ultimately a devotional about science.

It’s a devotional about God’s Word.

So let’s open our Bibles.

Genesis 1:1.

“In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.”


———-

Let me ask you something.

How seriously do you take the opening chapters of Genesis?

Because I think a lot of Christians have gotten into the habit of treating Genesis 1, 2, and 3 like they’re optional reading.

Like they’re just a children’s story we tell in Sunday school before getting to the important stuff.

But let me tell you something.

Genesis is the important stuff!

If Genesis is just a fairy tale, then what happens to the rest of redemptive history?

If Adam and Eve are fictional, if the Fall is fictional, if sin entering the world is fictional, then what exactly did Jesus Christ come to redeem us from?

What happens to Paul’s argument in Romans 5?

What happens to the connection between the first Adam and the last Adam in 1 Corinthians 15?

You see, I’m not arguing that every sentence in Genesis must be read without recognizing figures of speech. Scripture uses poetry, metaphor, and symbolism.

I’m asking whether we believe the events Scripture presents as the foundation of redemption actually happened.

Because if the foundation is fictitious, what happens to everything built upon it?

And here’s something else I want you to notice.

What did God originally give His creatures to eat?

Turn to Genesis 1:29–30.

God gives plants for food to mankind, and green plants to the animals.

Now, some of you might be thinking, “Hold on. Didn’t people eat animals?”

Well, let me ask you something.

Where does God explicitly give mankind permission to eat animals?

Anybody know?

Genesis 9:3.

After the Flood!

God tells Noah that every moving thing that lives shall be food for him, just as He had previously given him the green plants.

Now, that’s fascinating.

Why does Scripture describe these two provisions differently?

And how does that relate to the original goodness of creation, the Fall, and the curse?

These aren’t insignificant questions.

They’re questions about the very beginning of God’s redemptive history.

And I want you to understand something.

The Bible isn’t a collection of unrelated religious stories. It’s one unfolding account of God’s creation, man’s rebellion, God’s judgment, and God’s redemption through Jesus Christ.

It begins with creation.

It tells us how sin entered the world.

It reveals God’s promises.

It points us to Christ.

And it ends with the destruction of death, the removal of the curse, and the restoration of all things.

So please, don’t skip Genesis.

Don’t treat these chapters as if they’re irrelevant to your faith.

Because the God who speaks in Genesis 1 is the same God who raises the dead in Revelation.

And the Christ who conquers death in Revelation is the same Christ through whom all things were created in the beginning.


——-

I want you to think about something.

If there’s even one thing wrong in this book, how can I trust it?

How can I build my life upon it?

How can I be willing to die for it?

Think about the Christians throughout history who suffered and died because they refused to abandon their faith.

Think about William Tyndale.

In the 1500s, Tyndale devoted his life to translating the Scriptures into English so ordinary people could read the Word of God for themselves.

And in 1536, he was executed for heresy.

Think about John Rogers. Hugh Latimer. Nicholas Ridley. Thomas Cranmer.

Men who were willing to die rather than abandon what they believed God had revealed.

And that raises a question for every one of us.

What are you willing to die for? And what are you living for?

Because we have something extraordinary sitting right here in our hands.

The Word of God.

Sixty-six books, written across centuries, preserved and handed down through generations.

Think about what it must have been like for an ordinary English-speaking Christian in the sixteenth century to finally have access to Scripture in his own language.

Imagine holding that Bible for the first time.

Where would you begin?

Well, where do you begin when you pick up a book?

At the beginning!

So let’s do that.

Book one.

Chapter one.

Verse one.

“In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.”

Do you believe that?

Seriously. Do you believe that God created the heavens and the earth?

Okay.

Then let’s keep reading.

Because here’s something I want you to understand.

The God who created the universe didn’t need millions of years to accomplish His purposes.

He didn’t need thousands of years.

He didn’t even need six days.

He could have spoken everything into existence instantaneously!

In fact, one of the greatest theologians in Christian history, Augustine of Hippo, believed that God created everything in a single instant.

Now, I disagree with Augustine’s interpretation of the creation days.

But I love what his position illustrates about God’s omnipotence.

God is not limited by time, matter, or the physical laws He created.

So why six days?

Well, the Bible gives us a remarkable connection in Exodus 20:8–11.

God commands Israel to labor for six days and rest on the seventh, grounding that pattern in His own work of creation.

God establishes a pattern of work and rest for His people.

Isn’t that beautiful?

Now, here’s my question.

Why do so many of us struggle to accept six ordinary days?

Why are we so willing to introduce vast periods of time into the opening chapters of Genesis?

Some Christians place millions or billions of years between Genesis 1:1 and Genesis 1:2.

But where does the text actually tell us to do that?

What in the passage requires that interpretation?

I want us to examine those questions carefully.

Because I believe something has gone wrong when we become more concerned with making Scripture fit our understanding of the world than with allowing Scripture to correct our understanding.

And I want you to remember something.

There were eyewitnesses to creation.

Not human eyewitnesses.

The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—the one eternal, triune God—were present at creation.

John 1 tells us that all things were made through the Word.

Colossians 1 tells us that all things were created through Christ and for Christ.

And Genesis 1 tells us that the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters.

God was there. We were not.

Now, that doesn’t mean we should stop investigating the natural world. I love science. I love discovering the order God has established in His creation.

But it does mean that I want to approach Scripture with humility.

And here’s the question I want every Christian to consider.

When the conclusions we draw from nature appear to contradict our interpretation of Scripture, are we willing to examine both carefully?

Are we willing to let God’s Word correct us?

Because we’re about to encounter one of the most important declarations in all of Genesis.

At the end of the sixth day, God looks upon everything He has made.

And what does He say?

“Behold, it was very good.”

Now, I want you to think about that.

What does it mean for something to be good in the eyes of a perfectly holy God?

And how does that goodness relate to death, suffering, and the curse?

Because Scripture calls death an enemy.

Christ came to conquer death.

And Revelation promises a future in which death will be no more.

So here’s the question we’re going to wrestle with.

Was death part of God’s original good creation, or was it an enemy that entered through the Fall?

Let’s examine the Scriptures together.




Evolution is a proven, observable, undeniable fact of God’s creation.

And by the way, I’m Catholic.

Yeah, and I’d hope every Christian in this room is Catholic!

Have you ever heard the Apostles’ Creed?

You know that weird line in there, “I believe in the holy catholic church.”

What does catholic mean?

It means universal.

We’re talking about the universal Church of Jesus Christ, not the Roman Catholic Church that comes to mind so often when we hear that word, catholic.

that’s why terminology is so important.

Especially when we’re talking about things of such great importantance.

So, Evolution is an observable fact of nature, what does that mean? What do I mean by that?

What does evolution actually mean?

Because depending on who you’re talking to, people use the word evolution to describe some very different things.

I speaking with my father in law, Jess’s dad, Ben, and he’s got one of the strangest defaults I’ve ever come across. Ben hears the word evolution, and his mind is immediately drawn to the stars, stellar and planetary evolution, when you hear evolution, I’d assume that you think of THIS diagram right here, that shows an ape turning into a man. And I hate this graph, it misrepresents the macro evolutionist. See, evolution doesn’t claim we came from apes, it claims we share a common ancestor with apes. It also claims that we share a common ancestor with what you had for breakfast, I don’t mean the bacon or the eggs, I’m talking about the strawberries, the cantaloupe, the banana. evolutionists believe that we share a common ancestor with bananas. I’m not misrepresenting them, it’s true.

And if we’re going to have a serious conversation about creation, we need to make sure we’re actually talking about the same thing. Micro and macro, I hate that they made these terms sound so similar, Satan is extremely crafty. One definition of evolution explains the simple concept of the strong outcompeting the weak, and another definition seeks to destroy your faith. Only 1 letter apart here, isn’t Satan just a sneaky little bugger. One is observable, provable repeatable, and the other has absolutely not a shred of evidence supporting it, and it seeks to undermine the authority of God as you will soon hear about shortly.


——

Points I want to emphasize throughout:
- there’s no issue believing in all the years, the time, the issue is if you believe God had animals in pain & suffering & dying before Adam cast the world into sin
- If you ever encounter someone who truly believes in this ridiculous idea that there is no order to the universe, that, the universe chanced itself into existence, and that all the design in the universe that you observe, and even the mind in which you use to observe it, is all a great illusion. You just ask them this simple question. Could a tornado rip through a scrap yard, and build the Eiffel Tower? I’ve asked this question many times, and I always get the same answer from these macro evolutionists. They say “Yes, given enough time.” It’s foolish. It’s counter-biblical. See, the Bible makes a truth claim that this world is decaying, [insert scripture reference] Keep in mind how long ago that was written, and how very recently in history we’ve discovered entropy, a famous law of the universe that says The total disorder of an isolated system always increases over time. Things are naturally headed towards CHAOS. It’s the absolute polar opposite claim of the evolutionist who says, with time, and enough chaos, eventually, you just run into order. Who’s seen that before in their house? Yeah, you just life, the kids run around the house and throw their toys around, and eventually, given enough time, eventually the entire house finds its way back into order. If you just keep making messes, spilling drinks, breaking dishes, leaving dirty clothes around, if evolutionists were consistent, they would believe whole heartily that eventually their house would have enough chaos it in, that given enough time, their house would come across order & design. It’s something we’ve never once observed in our world. Never. Not once. Imagine I was smart enough to be pilot, and I was flying a plane over the oceans, and my co-pilot grabs me, and he says, Phil, am I seeing things? And I look down at an island, and on the beach there’s 3 big letter. SOS. And I turn to my co-pilot and say, “That is incredible, what are the odds of that? There’s SOS on the beach, what a crazy coincidence, do you know how rare that is for the water and the sand to shape out those letters, what would my co-pilot say. “YOU IDIOT. YOU FOOL. ARE YOU INTOXICATED? IT IS PLAIN TO SEE THAT A MIND WAS BEFORE WRITING THOSE LETTERS, THERE IS A CREATIVE MIND DOWN THERE ON THAT ISLAND RESPONSIBLE FOR WRITING THOSE 3 LETTERS. 3 letters, and it’s so obvious to anybody. And yet, our public school system, here in the United States, has brain washed several generations into thinking that the universe, our galaxy, our solar system, and our planet, and even your body, and your mind, came about by chance. You’re nothing but a walking bag of meat. This is the humanist perspective. This is NOT a perspective that we should marry into Christianity. This is not something that we look at, and say, let’s see how we can fit this into the Bible so that we’re not fighting the schools on this. We don’t wanna make a big issue about this cause, some people are just gonna think we’re dumb and we don’t like science. Are you trying to please man? Or are you trying to please God. If someone believes in both God and the origin
